name: cc1101-tool
firmware_note: Single Arduino sketch (not a full OS) that turns any supported board + CC1101 breakout into a serial-terminal-controlled sub-GHz transceiver. No GUI, no app - you type commands over a serial console.
price_note: No assembled unit is sold anywhere; this is parts cost only (Arduino Pro Micro clone ~$5-6, CC1101 breakout ~$4-6, wire). mcore1976 does not sell hardware - it is a firmware/wiring-diagram repo you build yourself.
skill_note: No PCB - you wire a CC1101 breakout to a Pro Micro (or ESP32/ESP8266/Nano/Pro Mini/RP2040) by hand following the repo's pinout photos, then flash the sketch and talk to it over a serial terminal. Nothing about the RF side is beginner-friendly; commands are typed, not menued.
build_note: Jumper-wire or solder a CC1101 breakout (E07-M1101D-SMA, D-SUN, or similar) to the chosen MCU per the repo's pinout diagrams, then flash with the Arduino IDE.
summary: An open-source Arduino sketch that drives a bare CC1101 breakout from a plain serial terminal - no Flipper, no SDR software, no proprietary app. It supports Pro Micro, Nano, Pro Mini, ESP32, ESP8266 and RP2040 as the host MCU, and the author positions it explicitly as a budget alternative to the YARD Stick One.
honest_take: This is genuinely a YARD Stick One competitor for people willing to build it themselves, and at $12 in parts versus roughly $200 for a YARD Stick One it is a real budget option - but you are trading a calibrated, driverless, GNU Radio-integrated tool for a hand-wired breakout and a text CLI with no official support channel beyond GitHub issues. It does the same fundamental things a Flipper Zero's sub-GHz app does (RX, TX, raw record/replay, jamming) using the identical CC1101 silicon, so if you already own a Flipper this buys you nothing except a dedicated headless box. The 'brute force' feature is fixed-code DIP-switch garage doors only - it does nothing against rolling codes, and the project makes no such claim.
best_for: Someone who wants a headless, low-cost CC1101 tool and is comfortable wiring their own hardware
Learning the CC1101's register-level behavior instead of hiding it behind a GUI
not_for: Anyone who wants an assembled, warrantied product
Rolling-code attacks - not supported
Beginners who haven't wired a breakout board before

radios.note: 300-348, 387-464 and 779-928 MHz. The repo lists compatible breakout boards (E07-M1101D-SMA, D-SUN and others) rather than shipping its own PCB.

hardware.storage: None - commands and captured frames live in the terminal session, not on the device
hardware.gpio: SPI to the CC1101 breakout; exact pins vary by supported MCU per the README's per-board pinout diagrams
hardware.case: None - bare board(s), typically breadboarded or dead-bug wired
notable_physical: No enclosure in any published build
Multiple wiring diagrams for different MCU choices

subghz_rx.note: Packet and raw-mode reception across the CC1101's three bands, controlled via serial commands.

subghz_tx.note: Packet and raw-mode transmission; modulation set via 2-FSK/GFSK/ASK-OOK/4-FSK/MSK commands matching CC1101 registers.

subghz_replay.note: RAW-mode record and replay of captured frames, which the author explicitly compares to Flipper Zero's raw sub-GHz replay.

subghz_bruteforce.note: Simulates DIP-switch garage-door codes only. Fixed-code systems, not rolling code.

subghz_rolling_code.note: No rolling-code (KeeLoq etc.) attack is implemented or claimed anywhere in the repo.

subghz_external_antenna.note: Depends entirely on which CC1101 breakout you wire up; SMA-equipped modules like the E07-M1101D-SMA are explicitly listed as compatible, but the tool itself adds nothing here.

subghz_amplified.note: The listed compatible breakouts (E07-M1101D-SMA, D-SUN) are plain CC1101 modules with no power amplifier, unlike PA-equipped modules such as the E07-433M20S used in amplified Flipper add-ons.

scriptable.note: Entirely command-driven over a serial terminal (PuTTY, Android USB-OTG terminal apps, or WiFi telnet on the ESP8266/ESP32 ports); there is also an IRC-like 'chat mode' between two units.

standalone_untethered.note: No screen or buttons - every function requires a connected terminal (serial or telnet).

usb_mass_storage.note: Not a feature of this sketch.

app_store.note: One GitHub repo, one sketch; no module/app ecosystem.

legal.notes: Building and owning the hardware is legal. Transmitting on sub-GHz ISM bands without the appropriate license/authorization, and replaying or brute-forcing signals for devices you don't own or control, are separately regulated (e.g. FCC Part 15 in the US) and can be a criminal offence depending on jurisdiction and target. Check your local law; this is not legal advice.

name: Flipper Zero SubGHz Module
firmware: n/a (passive RF front-end, no firmware of its own)
firmware_note: This is a radio module, not a firmware project. It runs whatever sub-GHz app the host Flipper Zero's own firmware (stock or Momentum/Unleashed/etc.) provides - the module changes the antenna/RF front end, not the software.
price_note: Sold in 400MHz and 900MHz band-matched versions, both listed as sold out. It also requires JCMK's separate $5 SPI Adapter Board (also sold out) to physically connect to the Flipper's GPIO header, so the real cost of the accessory is $17 when both are in stock.
skill_note: No soldering; it plugs onto the SPI Adapter Board, which plugs onto the Flipper's GPIO header.
build_note: Plug the module onto the required SPI Adapter Board, then onto the Flipper Zero's 18-pin GPIO header. No flashing needed - the Flipper's own sub-GHz app talks to it over SPI exactly as it does the internal CC1101.
summary: A standalone CC1101 module that plugs into a Flipper Zero's GPIO header (via a required separate adapter board) to externalize sub-GHz radio duties, so a bigger antenna or an amplifier can be attached instead of using the Flipper's small internal antenna. It does not add any new firmware capability - the Flipper's own sub-GHz app still runs the same features it always did.
honest_take: This is a single-radio accessory with no amplifier of its own, sold at the same price point as commodity 3-in-1 Flipper expansion boards that pack an ESP32 and an nRF24 alongside the same CC1101 - so buyers comparing on price alone are giving up two radios for the same money. If your actual goal is more transmit range, this module alone doesn't get you there; Rabbit-Labs' Flux Capacitor bundles a genuine +20 dBm power amplifier (E07-433M20S) into a similar GPIO board for about $59, versus this module's bare CC1101 with just a better antenna connector. Both the module and its required adapter board are currently sold out, so as of this check it isn't actually buyable at any price.

Attaching a directional or gain antenna without an amplifier
not_for: Anyone wanting more RF power - there's no PA here, see the Flux Capacitor instead

name: Open Source Meshtastic Nibble
firmware_note: Ships pre-flashed with mainline Meshtastic firmware, updatable over USB. Retia's own repo (github.com/retiallc/nibble) states the Nibble board variants are merged upstream into Meshtastic itself, rather than being a fork running divergent code.
price_note: All five listed variants (PCB only, unsoldered kit, and soldered/tested kit, each in RP2040 or ESP32-S3) are priced identically at $10 and all are currently sold out. That a fully assembled/tested unit costs the same as a bare PCB is unusual and confirmed directly on the live listing, not an error in our transcription.
skill_note: The unsoldered kit needs surface-mount-adjacent hand soldering (LoRa module, MCU module, LED); the Meshtastic side then needs comfort with mesh-network configuration (channels, PSK, node roles) which is not beginner territory even if the hardware is easy.
build_note: Soldered/tested variant is plug-and-play; the unsoldered kit is a small through-hole/module build designed to fit inside a 25mm PVC pipe for weatherproofing; PCB-only requires sourcing every part yourself from the published BOM.
summary: An open-source LoRa mesh-networking node built around an RFM95 (Semtech SX1276) radio and either an RP2040 or ESP32-S3, designed to fit inside a 1-inch PVC pipe for cheap weatherproof field deployment. It ships pre-loaded with mainline Meshtastic firmware, and the board design has been merged upstream into the Meshtastic project itself rather than being a one-off fork.
honest_take: This is not an offensive or defensive security tool - it's an encrypted off-grid mesh-comms node, useful to the same crowd that carries a Flipper because it solves 'no cell signal at a protest, a disaster site, or a remote con venue' rather than anything resembling a pentest primitive. It earns a place here because the comparison database already tracks general-purpose hacker-con hardware, and because Meshtastic mesh networks are exactly what some detection tooling elsewhere in this database (the MeshCore/Meshtastic detector keys) is built to spot - so a reader comparing detectors benefits from seeing what they're detecting. Buy the RP2040 version unless you specifically need BLE/Wi-Fi pairing with a phone: the ESP32-S3 variant burns meaningfully more power for that convenience. Every variant is currently sold out.
best_for: Off-grid encrypted mesh comms for field work, cons, or emergency use
Anyone who wants to understand what a Meshtastic detector in another device is actually matching on
not_for: Offensive security testing - it has no attack capability of any kind
Anyone needing GPS-tagged mesh logging out of the box - no GPS is included

name: Diabolic Parasite
firmware_note: Partially open source - the schematic is public and select firmware components are being released to GitHub, but the full firmware is not fully open at time of writing. Firmware v2.0 added 'Diabolic Shell', an encrypted bidirectional command/exfil channel over the same HID keystroke-reflection technique used for keylogging.
price_note: Crowdfunded (482% funded), orders placed now ship Oct 31, 2026. Plus $8 US / $18 worldwide shipping.
skill_note: Deploying it well requires physical access to swap a target's existing keyboard/mouse cable, understanding of USB HID descriptor behavior, and operational awareness of what its keystroke-injection and exfiltration channel will and won't trigger in EDR/behavioral tooling.
build_note: Fully assembled; a 3D-printable enclosure design was published separately in Feb 2026.
summary: An inline USB pass-through implant: you unplug a target's keyboard/mouse, plug it into the Parasite's female port, then plug the Parasite into the freed host port. It clones the passthrough device's full USB identity (VID/PID/manufacturer/product strings), logs every keystroke to a web UI over Wi-Fi, and can be wirelessly triggered to inject keystrokes or open an encrypted covert shell - all while behaving as an inert passthrough the rest of the time.
honest_take: The headline feature isn't the keystroke injection - every device in this batch does that - it's that Diabolic Parasite is simultaneously a full hardware keylogger for whatever real keyboard is plugged through it, which almost none of the cheaper BadUSB cables/sticks here can do. That capability is also exactly why it's the most legally dangerous device in this batch: wiretapping/keylogger statutes in most jurisdictions treat *capturing someone else's input* very differently from injecting your own, and 'Diabolic Shell' turning stray keystrokes into a live exfiltration channel is squarely built for interactive access to systems you don't own. It's still pre-order as of this check (ships Oct 31, 2026, per the vendor), so nothing about its real-world detectability against modern EDR is independently verified yet - treat vendor evasion claims as marketing until someone publishes a teardown or a blue-team writeup.

Simulating a compromised peripheral for insider-threat exercises
not_for: Anyone without explicit written authorization - keylogging a third party's real keyboard traffic is a separate, often more serious, legal exposure than keystroke injection alone
Buying today - it's still pre-order, not shipping

name: Diabolic Drive
firmware_note: June 2025 firmware update added keystroke reflection/exfiltration, dynamic hardware-ID spoofing and OS detection. ATmega32U4 side supports 'almost any open source firmware built for those chips' - the vendor names WiFi Duck, WiFi Ducky, ESPloitV2, WHID and supremeDuck as compatible alternatives, since the ATmega32U4 and ESP8266 are wired over Serial/I2C the same way those projects expect.
price_note: In stock, ships within three business days. Plus $8 US / $18 worldwide shipping.
skill_note: Default operation (plug in, trigger a stored payload over the web UI) is approachable; spoofing hardware IDs, writing custom firmware, or using the exposed ATmega32U4 bootloader for deep customization is not.
build_note: Ships fully assembled and tested in a universal flash-drive PCB form factor meant to be dropped into a generic flash-drive enclosure.
summary: A USB-A flash drive that is a genuine, working 64GB storage device (real read/write, ~20/10 Mbps) until wirelessly commanded over its own Wi-Fi access point to expose a HID keyboard interface and fire a stored keystroke-injection payload. Both its storage and HID personas can have their VID/PID/serial/vendor strings spoofed to match a specific brand.
honest_take: This is the most direct like-for-like comparison in the batch: the vendor's own listing puts it against the Rubber Ducky ($100, no wireless, no storage) and O.MG Cable Basic ($120, wireless but no 64GB of real storage) and the pricing genuinely tracks - you're paying about the same as those for meaningfully more (dual persona, real usable storage that works *during* payload firing, spoofable IDs). The catch is architectural, not marketing: it's an ATmega32U4 doing the HID work talking to an ESP8266 over serial/I2C, the same pairing used by several $25 hobbyist boards in this very batch (Wifi BadUSB, and the open-source WiFi Duck/supremeDuck lineage it's explicitly compatible with) - so a chunk of the $115 is the 64GB flash controller, the assembled/tested universal-drive PCB, and spoofable-ID firmware polish, not exotic silicon.

Red teams wanting spoofable hardware IDs on both the storage and HID personas
not_for: Anyone who wants the cheapest possible wireless BadUSB - the ATmega32U4+ESP8266 hobbyist boards in this batch do the injection side for a quarter of the price, just without real usable storage

name: USB Nugget (ESP32-S2)

summary: A defensive inline USB dongle, not an attack tool: it sits between your device and an untrusted host or charger, and lets you cut the USB data lines entirely ('anti-juice-jacking' data integrity mode) while separately capping current at one of five selectable thresholds (0.5-2.4A) and hard-clamping over-voltage at 6.5V to protect against a faulty or malicious power source.
honest_take: This solves a real, narrow problem - juice-jacking and dodgy charging ports - and does it with genuinely open, inspectable hardware (schematic, PCB layout and firmware are all public), which is more than most of the covert attack tools in this batch can say. It is not a general USB firewall: it does nothing against a device that already has a valid, unblocked data connection, and the over-voltage protection is fixed at 6.5V by hardware, not adjustable. It occupies the same defensive niche as the O.MG UnBlocker already in this database; UsbSafe2 predates it by years and adds current/voltage protection that the UnBlocker doesn't claim, but doesn't have the UnBlocker's more polished branding or O.MG ecosystem integration.

summary: An ATmega32U4 USB stick paired with a JDY-08 Bluetooth 4.0 module, remotely triggerable over BLE to fire DuckyScript-compatible keystroke/mouse-injection payloads via the open-source supremeDuck firmware. It has been sold out since 2019.
honest_take: This is the BLE sibling of the same maker's Wifi BadUSB, using identical core silicon (ATmega32U4) with a different radio bolted on, and the honest headline is that it's been unavailable for seven years - this belongs in the database as a documented historical/reference design rather than something to actually go buy. Its JDY-08 module is explicitly BLE 4.0 only and the listing warns it will not connect to a phone that only supports BLE 4.2, which is itself a sign of the module's age; the maker's own comparison notes it has no BLE pairing password at all, and its ~5m range is the shortest of the maker's three variants (WiFi and the JDY-10 BLE variant both reach roughly 14m). If BLE-triggered BadUSB is what you're after today, expect to build this yourself from the open EasyEDA files rather than purchase an assembled unit.

summary: An ATmega32U4 USB stick paired with an ESP-12F Wi-Fi module, hosting its own access point ('supremeDuck' by default) for wireless keystroke-injection control. It's compatible with three different open-source firmware options (supremeDuck, wifi_ducky, ESPloitV2) since its ATmega32U4+ESP-12F hardware pairing matches what all three projects target.
honest_take: This is the direct $25 open-source ancestor of the architecture Diabolic Drive charges $115 for elsewhere in this batch: both pair an ATmega32U4 for HID injection with an ESP-series Wi-Fi chip over serial, both run DuckyScript-compatible payloads, and both host a self-controlled Wi-Fi AP. What the $115 device adds - real usable 64GB storage that works simultaneously with injection, spoofable VID/PID/serial on both personas, and an assembled/tested/supported product - is real, but so is the roughly 4.5x price gap for what is architecturally the same trick. The maker's own comparison notes the Wi-Fi version has 'occasional lag spikes in mouse movement' and is less reliable than the BLE variants, and reflashing the ESP-12F requires a NodeMCU-style flasher rather than a simple drag-and-drop. This one has been sold out since 2023, and the default AP password ('37373737') is published in the product listing, so anyone buying a used or self-built unit should change it before relying on it for anything sensitive.

name: Mouse Jiggler
firmware_note: Not open source; sold as a finished product with no published firmware source. Functionally the same idea as numerous open-source ATtiny85/Digispark mouse-jiggler projects on GitHub, but this specific unit's internals are not confirmed to match any of them.

summary: A USB device that enumerates as a generic mouse and injects small, randomized cursor movements referenced back to the original position, purely to prevent screensaver/idle-lock/sleep from triggering. It is not an attack tool - it's an operational-support accessory used during physical or remote engagements (or ordinary desk use) to keep a session from locking.
honest_take: This is the simplest, most single-purpose device in the entire batch, and that's fine - it does exactly one narrow thing and the vendor doesn't oversell it. The common misconception is that 'mouse jiggler' implies something clever defeating enterprise idle-detection; in reality this is a generic HID mouse sending small relative movements, and independent security-vendor writeups describe exactly this class of device being flagged by modern EDR (naming CrowdStrike, SentinelOne and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) via synthetic-movement timing analysis or known jiggler HID/VID-PID signatures - so treat 'undetectable' marketing claims skeptically in a monitored enterprise environment even though the movement itself is genuinely imperceptible to a human eye. No MCU, firmware source, or internal design is published by the vendor, unlike the open-source ATtiny85/Digispark mouse-jiggler projects that do the same thing for a few dollars in parts if you're willing to build one.
